name: Waist trainer
lead: A waist trainer is a tight, corset-style garment, usually of elastic fabric with rigid or semi-rigid boning, worn around the midsection to compress it. Modern products are marketed for daily wear over weeks or months with the aim of narrowing the waist, and they circulate widely on image-focused social media. They are descendants of the historical corset and of mid-twentieth-century waist cinchers.[1]

The visible slimming while the garment is worn comes from compression and redistribution of soft tissue. Claims of lasting fat loss or permanent reshaping are made by sellers and by many wearers, while published research on the topic is sparse. Historical and physiological work on corsets, including studies using reenactors who wore corsets, has examined effects on breathing,[2] and a medical-history summary reports that moderately laced corsets reduced lung capacity.[1]
infobox: Around the lower ribs and abdomen

paras: Contemporary waist trainers are usually made of latex or fabric blends with a hook-and-eye or zip closure and plastic or steel stays. They are shorter and more elastic than historical corsets, which were generally made of stiffer materials and were laced rather than hooked. The Wikipedia article on corsets notes that elasticated waist trainers and girdles are still worn and serve a similar shaping purpose, but lack the rigidity of boned corsets.[1]

The Wikipedia article on corsets reports evidence of corset use in Minoan Crete, the use of boned stays among European aristocrats from the late sixteenth century, the introduction of metal eyelets in 1827 that made tight lacing possible, and the use of steel boning from about 1850.[1] It reports that elastic materials from 1911 helped girdles replace corsets, that waist cinchers were revived in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and that corsets were again fashionable in periodic revivals from the late 1980s.[1] The article gives average corseted waists in the 1880s of about 53 cm against about 69 cm unlaced.[1]

Modern waist trainers are promoted through social media, where wearers post before-and-after images and describe daily wear schedules. The sources consulted here do not document the precise origin of the modern product category.

A waist trainer applies circumferential pressure. While worn, soft tissue is displaced above and below the band and the abdominal wall is compressed, which narrows the silhouette. No mechanism for lasting fat loss or permanent change to the rib cage during adult use has been established in published studies. The Wikipedia article on corsets reports that corseting in childhood and adolescence appeared to alter the spine, ribs and hips permanently, and that long-term use was linked to weakened core and back muscles, based on historical observations rather than controlled trials.[1]

The historical medical literature, as summarised on Wikipedia, reports that moderately laced corsets reduced lung capacity by 2 to 29 per cent, with an average of 9 per cent, and increased breathlessness during exercise.[1] Physicians of the Victorian period also proposed links between tight lacing and digestive disturbance, pelvic organ prolapse and other effects, though the article describes some evidence on these as mixed.[1] The same article describes as baseless the belief that Victorian women commonly had ribs removed to achieve smaller waists.[1]

A 2018 Iowa State University repository record titled "Historic medical perspectives of corseting and two physiologic studies with reenactors" addresses the physiology of corset wearing.[2] Wearers of modern trainers commonly report discomfort and restricted deep breathing; product sellers typically state that users should build up wear time gradually.
Waist trainers are discussed in appearance communities as a way to emphasise a narrow waist and a hip-to-waist contrast, and are most visible in fashion and influencer content.

No studies found on modern waist trainers for lasting waist reduction. Related research includes a 2018 university repository record that reports on historical medical perspectives on corseting and two physiologic studies with reenactors wearing corsets.[2]

timeline.event: Metal eyelets are introduced, making tight lacing of corsets practical.[1]
Steel boning becomes popular in corsets.[1]
Elastic materials begin to help girdles replace corsets.[1]
Waist cinchers are briefly revived alongside Dior's New Look.[1]
